claims.text: Local elemental segregation in high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles creates regions of reduced cohesive bonding.
Regions with reduced cohesive bonding act as nucleation sites for premelting.
Nanoparticles with a more homogeneous elemental distribution and minimal short-range order have delayed premelting onset relative to compositionally segregated nanoparticles.
Nanoparticles with a more homogeneous elemental distribution have higher melting temperatures than compositionally segregated nanoparticles.
Rapid quenching maximizes compositional uniformity and minimizes chemical short-range ordering in high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles.
Post-synthesis annealing can induce mild chemical short-range ordering or elemental segregation in high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles.
Local chemical short-range order or segregation changes interatomic bonding energies at nanoparticle surfaces and interfaces.
Localized compositional fluctuations reduce local binding energies and promote atomistic disorder at lower temperatures.
A homogeneous elemental distribution maximizes configurational-entropy stabilization.
Configurational-entropy stabilization postpones surface disorder and subsequent melting in high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles.
Segregated nanoparticles will exhibit earlier surface-premelting features and lower melting temperatures than the homogeneous baseline.
High-entropy-alloy nanoparticles relevant to the proposed hypothesis are typically 5–50 nm in diameter.
High-entropy-alloy nanoparticles are used in sensing applications.
Particle size, surface morphology, and synthesis kinetics may limit the applicability of the proposed segregation-controlled melting mechanism.
The magnitude of the premelting or melting-temperature shift may depend on particle-size distribution, surface faceting, and synthesis-related kinetic effects.
